summary:
Long-duration missions require autonomous health monitoring, as communication with Earth will have significant delays (approx. 29 mins on Mars). Team DZAT have developed an educational web-based application called Body in Space that enables crew members to monitor their health.
The application provides answers to three questions: What changed? Where is the problem? What should I look at? It shows vital signs, personal baselines and mission data using an interactive body diagram covering nine different health and environmental areas. The application provides references. The standard NEWS2 score is shown alongside each person's 7-day personal baseline. This means crew members can identify any changes to their health even if they have a low standard score. Crew members can log their measurements, run quick checks and complete a step-by-step emergency pathway.
The application uses guidance from NASA's human health resources. The Lab Explorer tool can be used to explore published data from the Inspiration4 mission in NASA's Open Science Data Repository. Wearable data is currently simulated. The next stages will involve clinical review, validation and sensor integration to provide greater autonomy to space crews and those in isolated environments on Earth.
details:
The source code, setup instructions, and references are publicly available on GitHub:
https://github.com/Volnikus/Bodyinspacenew

Astronauts need to identify changes in their health during a long mission when experiencing changes in gravity, radiation, isolation and reduced access to medical support. This increases the difficulty of this task when there is a delay in communication. The earliest response from Earth in our Mars transit scenario is a round-trip communication delay of about 29 minutes.

Body in Space is built around three questions:
What changed? Where is the problem? What should I look at?

This allows users to explore a body map with 8 health/environment sections. When clicking on each section you can view different metrics, trends, why they have changed and information based on the source. This includes: Brain/Mind, Eyes, Heart, Lungs, Blood, Bones and Muscles, Temperature, Air Quality & Radiation.
This uses a traditional NEWS2 scoring system but also compares against a personal baseline. In our demo we have shown an example where the crew member has a heart rate about 24% above their personal baseline compared to their normal levels. However, the NEWS2 score stays at 0. This helps provide visibility that even though the score is low not every metric is within normal levels for this person. The rules for the baselines are prototype and will need to be validated.
Users can add a new metric and instantly see their new assessment. It also includes tools to test your reaction, vision, breathing and mood. KOMEK (local rule-based agent) provides explanations based on a static knowledge library. It also includes reminders.

SOS Training
A step-by-step guide with a CPR metronome and a log of the actions taken. The mission settings allow you to change the delay, evacuation options and environment. The main functionality for monitoring and providing advice is designed to work offline. However, any updated information from outside the application will require internet.

Lab Explorer
This provides access to published observations from Inspiration4 from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.
The application was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Zustand. Data is stored in the browser’s local storage, and automated tests run with Vitest.
This aims to make health information more easily understood when there isn't instant expert support. The current version is a prototype for educational purposes. To develop it further, it would need physician review, usability testing, validation of the assessment rules and integration with real sensors.
dataRefs: NASA OSDR OSD-569: Published Inspiration4 complete blood count data, displayed in the laboratory explorer.
NASA OSDR OSD-575: Published Inspiration4 comprehensive metabolic panel data, used to explore changes across preflight and postflight measurements.
NASA Human Research Program: Human-spaceflight hazards and health-risk resources informed the body-system explanations and mission context.
NASA-STD-3001 and OCHMO technical briefs: References for medical operations, cabin carbon dioxide, radiation protection, sleep and nutrition.
NASA research on Mars communication delays and Earth-Independent Medical Operations: Informed the delayed-Earth-link scenario and the emphasis on crew autonomy.
NASA DONKI: Integrated as an external source of solar-flare and coronal-mass-ejection information, with cached results for offline access.

ISS Medical Checklist / Emergency Manual (public release, 2016): Referenced when developing the emergency training flow. Public copy hosted by GovernmentAttic. The prototype’s adaptation has not been clinically reviewed.
projectRefs: Canadian Space Agency — Bio-Monitor: Informed the selection of parameters represented in the simulated wearable feed.
ESA/IBMP — Mars-500: Referenced for isolation and sleep context.
Royal College of Physicians — NEWS2: Source of the conventional early-warning score.
PUCRS MicroG Centre research: The Evetts-Russomano CPR method informed microgravity-specific emergency content. This is a research reference, not a Brazilian Space Agency dataset.
